items.title: Bobby Watson interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, January 19, 1996
items.q: People like Lou Donaldson and Barry Harris, they’re in our generation, a lot of them just started going to Europe maybe ten years ago for the first time in their life.

ctx.x: I’m going to ask you one thing, and I know we’ve got to get you out of here because you’ve got to get something to eat and get dressed and maybe detox a little bit. But where is jazz going? Give me some places where it can go, or the possibilities that you see in it.

Well, I think we have to stop categorizing. Like now you know I’m doing this electric thing, and because I grew up doing it. But also I play jazz. And so you’re going to hear my things be a little bit more aggressive than what they call that soft jazz. Because we’re still up there really trying to mesh and play. But that’s not all I do. Like I mentioned earlier, I play in the church so I’d like to do a Gospel record at some point. And here’s another thing I see that really has changed the dynamics of the music.…

play. They can really play. You can not say that jazz is American anymore. Jazz started in America, particularly by black people. But now it has spread throughout the world and has become a proven formula. And it’s transcended all racial, sexual and religious nationalistic lines, that if you submit to the music, you will have success, and be able to get to what you’re saying inside. Because now there are young kids from other countries that understand what this music is about. So now, when me and my generations…
